unit-m3r.title: Topic 3 · Topic Review
unit-m3r.source: enVision Math, Topic 3 textbook scan — Lessons 3-1 to 3-7 (Drive)

summary.text: The whole of Topic 3 in one pool: exponents and powers of 10, place value through millions, decimals to thousandths, equivalent decimals and their forms, comparing and ordering, rounding, and decimal-chart structure — served as mixed rounds so the skills interleave.

why.text: A topic test asks everything at once, so practice should too. Deciding WHICH skill a question wants — exponent pattern, padding, rounding band — is itself the tested skill, and only mixed rounds train it.

objectives.text: Move between exponent, standard, expanded and word forms in both directions.
Compare, order and squeeze between decimals by padding to equal length.
Round decimals in one step and reason backwards from a rounded result.
Use the ×10-per-seat structure to explain, not just compute.

parentNote.text: The capstone for Topic 3. The three-level questions lean hard on critique-reasoning — Kavya, Milo, and the hidden-digit items are where understanding shows. If the mixed rounds go well, she is ready for whatever the class calls the Topic 3 test.

nextUp.text: Two or three mixed rounds across different days beats one long sitting — the shuffle is the point.

cards.def:
**Everything in this topic is a single place-value chart, read left or right of the point.**
• Exponents name the big seats; thousandths name the small ones.
• Every seat is worth 10 times its right-hand neighbour.
cards.hint: One ladder. Powers of 10 go up it; decimals go down it.

cards.def:
**The exponent counts the 10s, and equals the zeros in the product.**
• 10⁵ = 100,000. And 6 × 10⁴ = 60,000.
cards.hint: Count zeros ↔ read exponent, both directions.

cards.def:
**Decimal places match the zeros in the denominator.**
• 0.083 = 83/1,000 — three places, three zeros.
cards.hint: Places = zeros. Pad the front, never the back.

cards.def:
**End zeros are free; a zero between the point and the digits changes everything.**
• 2.5 = 2.50 = 2.500, but 2.05 is a different number.
cards.hint: WHERE the zero sits is the entire question.

cards.def:
**Stack the points, pad to equal length, first differing seat wins.**
• 12.8 vs 12.68 → 12.80 vs 12.68 → tenths decide.
cards.hint: Pad, then walk left to right. Stop at the first disagreement.

cards.def:
**Mark the seat, let the next digit vote (5 up), drop the tail — in ONE step.**
• 448 to the nearest hundred is 400, never via 450.
cards.hint: One look, one decision, no chaining.

cards.def:
**Across is the small step; down is ten of them; rows end on a rollover.**
• Two paths to a cell must agree — that is your check.
cards.hint: Walk the chart; don't compute it.

questions.q: A warehouse stores 7 × 10⁴ boxes. How many boxes is that?
questions.hint: Attach as many zeros as the exponent.
steps: Check: the product keeps exactly four zeros, matching the exponent.

ex.main: **70,000.** Four zeros follow the 7.
ex.tip: The 28 trap is 7 × 4 — the exponent never multiplies directly.

questions.q: What is the value of the 5 in 2,571,368?
questions.hint: Find the seat before the value.
steps: Count seats from the right: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, hundred-thousands.
The 5 lands in the hundred-thousands seat.

ex.main: **500,000.** The seat multiplies the digit.
ex.tip: Value questions are seat questions in disguise.

questions.q: Which decimal equals 6/1,000?
questions.hint: Three zeros in the denominator, three decimal places.
steps: Thousandths means exactly three decimal places.
006 fills them: 0.006 — the front zeros hold the seats.

ex.main: **0.006.** Pad the front to fill the seats.
ex.tip: Places and zeros always match — count them both.

questions.q: Which decimal is equivalent to 8.20?
questions.hint: Which option only drops an END zero?
steps: 8.20's final zero is after the last nonzero digit — free.
Dropping it gives 8.2, the same number.
Say both: "twenty hundredths", "two tenths" — the same amount twice.

ex.main: **8.2.** Twenty hundredths is two tenths.
ex.tip: 8.02 moves the 2 to a different seat — that zero is load-bearing.

questions.q: Two snail trails measure 0.54 m and 0.6 m. Which comparison is true?

ex.main: **0.6 > 0.54.** The shorter-written decimal is the bigger number here.
ex.tip: Pad first and the illusion disappears.

questions.q: What is 7.85 rounded to the nearest whole number?
steps: One right: 8, which is 5 or more.

ex.main: **8.** The 8 in the tenths votes up.
ex.tip: Whole-number rounding drops the decimal point entirely.

questions.q: A national park recorded 4,060,000 visitors. Which is its expanded form using exponents?
steps: The 4 is in the millions seat: 4 × 10⁶.
The 6 is in the ten-thousands seat: 6 × 10⁴.

ex.main: **(4 × 10⁶) + (6 × 10⁴).** Two filled seats, two terms.
ex.tip: Silent seats appear in standard form as zeros and in expanded form not at all.

questions.q: How is "three and nine hundredths" written as a decimal?

ex.main: **3.09.** The zero holds the tenths seat.
ex.tip: 3.9 would be "three and nine TENTHS" — the seat name matters.

questions.q: In 44,000, how do the two 4s compare?
opts: The left 4 is worth 10 times the right 4
The left 4 is worth 100 times the right 4
The right 4 is worth 10 times the left 4
steps: One seat apart: a factor of exactly 10.

ex.main: **10 times.** Adjacent seats always differ by one factor of 10.
ex.tip: Two seats apart would make it 100 — the steps stack.

questions.q: Which number sits between 7.1 and 7.2?
steps: The others land outside the band.

ex.main: **7.15.** Zoom one seat deeper and the room appears.
ex.tip: Between any two unequal decimals there is always another — always.

questions.q: A stopwatch shows 58.276 seconds. What is the time to the nearest hundredth?

ex.main: **58.28 s.** The 6 votes up and vanishes.
ex.tip: Race times round to hundredths for exactly this reason — carrying the units matters.

questions.q: In a hundredths chart, one cell is reached going right from 0.67 or down from 0.58. What is in it?

ex.main: **0.68.** Two roads, one cell.
ex.tip: When the two paths disagree, the error is yours, not the chart's.

questions.q: Which equation is FALSE?
questions.hint: Count each option's zeros against its exponent.

ex.main: **9 × 10³ = 90,000 is the false one.** Three zeros make 9,000.
ex.tip: Hunting the FALSE statement forces you to verify all four — that is the point.

questions.q: Kavya says 0.480 is greater than 0.48 "because it has more digits". What should you tell her?
opts: She is right — longer decimals are greater
They are equal — the extra zero is after the last nonzero digit
They cannot be compared without a number line
questions.hint: Is that zero free or load-bearing?
steps: End zeros rename tenths/hundredths into thousandths without changing the amount.

ex.main: **They are equal.** Written length says nothing about size.
ex.tip: The same instinct wrongly says 12.68 > 12.8 — padding fixes both.

questions.q: A number rounds to 6.3 to the nearest tenth AND to 6.28 to the nearest hundredth. Which could it be?
questions.hint: Two bands must overlap — solve each, then intersect.
steps: Nearest hundredth 6.28 needs: 6.275 up to but not including 6.285.
Nearest tenth 6.3 needs: 6.25 up to but not including 6.35.
6.251 rounds to 6.25; 6.292 rounds to 6.29; 6.234 rounds to 6.23 and 6.2 — each fails a band.

ex.main: **6.283.** Inside the 6.28 band, which itself sits inside the 6.3 band.
ex.tip: Two rounding facts about one number are two overlapping bands — the answer lives in the overlap.

questions.q: Milo claims that moving a digit two seats left multiplies its value by 20. What should you tell him?
opts: The factor depends on which digit moves
He is right — two seats, 10 each, makes 20
Two seats left divides the value by 100
Each seat multiplies by 10, so two seats multiply by 100

ex.main: **× 100, not × 20.** Place-value steps multiply; they never add.
ex.tip: His error is treating a multiplicative ladder like an additive one — the single deepest misconception in this topic.

questions.q: Which list is ordered from least to greatest?
steps: That ascending order is exactly the first list.

ex.main: **0.098, 0.9, 0.908, 0.98.** Padded, the order is just integer order.
ex.tip: Every wrong list here trips on 0.9 looking small — padding is the cure.

questions.q: A relay team's four splits, in seconds, were 12.06, 12.6, 12.066, and 12.61. The anchor ran the FASTEST split. Which time was the anchor's?
questions.hint: Fastest means smallest — pad to thousandths.

ex.main: **12.06 s.** Smaller time, faster runner — and 12.06 < 12.066 by six thousandths.
ex.tip: Fastest-vs-greatest is a reading question stacked on a math question. Read first.

questions.q: Round 9.996 to the nearest hundredth.
questions.hint: The vote forces a cascade of rollovers.
steps: The zeros after the point show the precision you rounded to.

ex.main: **10.00.** The round-up ripples through every 9.
ex.tip: Keeping the two zeros records that you rounded to hundredths — 10 alone loses that.

questions.q: One digit of 5.7■4 is hidden. Rounded to the nearest hundredth, the number is 5.72. What is the hidden digit?
questions.hint: The 4 in the thousandths votes DOWN.
steps: The thousandths digit is 4 — less than 5 — so rounding leaves the hundredths digit alone.
After rounding, the hundredths digit reads 2.
Since nothing changed, the hidden digit IS 2.

ex.main: **2.** A down-vote means the rounded digit was never touched.
ex.tip: Running the rounding machine backwards is the surest test you understand it forwards.

questions.q: A thousandths chart row ends …0.038, 0.039, ■. What completes the row?
steps: 0.040 = 0.04 — the rolled-over hundredth ends the row.
The next row then opens at 0.041.

ex.main: **0.04.** Forty thousandths is four hundredths.
ex.tip: The short-looking answer is the rollover in disguise — every row ends with one.

questions.q: Order these from least to greatest.
questions.hint: Turn everything into standard form first.

ex.main: **300, 3,200, 30,000, 300,000.** Convert first, order second.
ex.tip: Mixed representations are only hard until everything speaks standard form.

questions.q: Which number is one-tenth of 4.7?
steps: One-tenth slides each digit one seat right.

ex.main: **0.47.** The ladder works in both directions.
ex.tip: 47 is the ×10 answer — the direction of the slide is the whole question.

questions.q: Which fraction equals 0.219?
steps: Count the places right of the point: three.

ex.main: **219/1,000.** Three places, three zeros.
ex.tip: The denominator is readable straight off the number of places.
